section.title: Representing functions by power series
section.p: The last section gave us permission to work with power series inside their radius of convergence. We can add, multiply, differentiate, and integrate them term by term.
Now we use that permission in the opposite direction.
Instead of starting with a power series and asking where it converges, we start with a function and ask:

exercise.title: Why is a power series representation an identity together with an interval?

statement.p: The geometric series gives 1/(1-x)=1+x+x^2+\cdots only for |x|<1. In your own words, why is the interval part of the mathematics rather than a footnote, and why is the formula false at x=2 even though the left side is defined there?

hint.p: The right side is a limit of partial sums. Outside |x|<1 those partial sums do not approach the function, so the two sides are not the same object.

exercise.title: How can one seed series grow new representations?

statement.p: Once the geometric series is known, substitution, differentiation, and integration produce series for other functions. In your own words, why must a substitution keep the new inner expression inside the original radius, and why do differentiated or integrated series keep the radius but not the endpoints?

hint.p: Replacing x by u(x) is legal only where |u(x)|<1. Calculus operations are justified inside the radius; the endpoints are a separate numerical question after the operation.

statement.p: Integrating the series for 1/(1+x) produces the series for \ln(1+x) on (-1,1]. In your own words, why is the identity first proved only inside the radius, and why is the endpoint x=1 a separate argument rather than an automatic gift?

hint.p: Term-by-term integration is guaranteed in the open interval. At x=1 the series becomes the alternating harmonic series, whose convergence and identification with \ln 2 need their own reasons.

note.title: Computational lesson
note.p: A series representation is not only a formula. It is also an algorithm. Its usefulness depends on how fast its terms shrink.

subsection.p: The geometric series gave us logarithms and inverse tangents. But the functions
do not obviously come from the geometric series. To reach them, we need a new question:
subsection.md: \text{Can the derivatives of a function tell us which polynomial should approximate it?}
subsection.p: That question leads to Taylor polynomials.

exercise.title: Why can a slowly convergent series still be the right idea?

statement.p: The Leibniz series for \pi/4 is beautiful but slow, while arctangent at smaller inputs is faster. In your own words, why does a series representation become a computational tool, and why does using the same series closer to its center change the efficiency?

hint.p: A series is useful only where its remainder is controllable. Smaller inputs make powers shrink faster, so the same identity can be a poor calculator or a good one depending on where it is evaluated.
